proposal: The Mandate says CISA's funding should align narrowly with protecting federal civilian networks and coordinating critical infrastructure security, that its counter-misinformation and disinformation work should end immediately and its Cybersecurity Advisory Committee be dismissed on day one, and that its election role be limited to hygiene assessments. status_summary: Parts of the narrowing are operative and parts are only proposed: CISA lost about a third of its workforce after January 2025 (Cybersecurity Dive, 2026-02-12), election-security and foreign-influence/disinformation staff were reported placed on administrative leave in a state official's letter of 2025-02-12, and DHS ended all advisory committee memberships on 2025-01-20 (sources reviewed name the Cyber Safety Review Board but not the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee). The FY2027 CISA justification (reported 2026-04-07; not enacted) requests $2,487,194K, 2,865 positions and 2,528 FTE, 385.8 million dollars and 867 positions below the FY2026 annualized continuing resolution; it would end the 14-position, 39.6 million dollar election security program (the advisors in all ten regions and EI-ISAC funding), end CFATS (223 positions, 35.1 million dollars) because its statutory authorities expired, discontinue the Bombing Prevention budget line and shift some school safety programs to states and localities, and Cybersecurity Dive also reports closure of the Stakeholder Engagement Division. The justification never uses the words misinformation or disinformation, so SecurityWeek's report of a 707 million dollar cut ending counter-misinformation programs is its own characterization; CRS R48979 (2026-06-09) puts the 386 million dollar gap against the FY2025 continuing-resolution level. No proposal to move CISA to Transportation or emergency communications to FEMA was found, and CFATS would end rather than move to FEMA; in June 2026 DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin described structural change while seeking up to 600 more staff. On 2026-09-24 CISA released a 2026 election infrastructure security plan that relies on regional directors and threat-sharing tools and does not restore dedicated election adviser positions, per Nextgov.

timeline.event: Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman issues a memo ending all memberships on DHS advisory committees, effective immediately; reports name the Cyber Safety Review Board and do not name the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.

A letter from Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs to the state's congressional delegation reports that CISA employees in its Election Security and Resilience Division and its Foreign Influence Operations and Disinformation initiative were placed on administrative leave, and describes uncertainty over federal funding for the election-focused information sharing center (EI-ISAC).

Cybersecurity Dive reports CISA has lost about a third of its workforce since January 2025 and is preparing a Cybersecurity Division reorganization that will turn off some programs and prioritize operational technology security, cyber intelligence and collaborative defense.
DHS funding lapse begins; congressional testimony cited by CRS says CISA furloughed roughly 60 percent of staff. P.L. 119-86, enacted 2026-04-30, ended the lapse for most of DHS including CISA.

The FY2027 budget request proposes cutting about $707 million from CISA (to roughly $2 billion), dissolving the stakeholder-engagement and international affairs offices, terminating programs focused on countering misinformation and propaganda, and removing school safety initiatives; a separate outlet reports it would also eliminate the election security program and shift some infrastructure security and emergency communications responsibilities to state and local governments. SecurityWeek reports Congress had cut the proposed FY2026 reduction from $491 million to about $135 million.

Cybersecurity Dive reports that the FY2027 CISA budget justification would cut a net 386 million dollars and 867 positions (leaving 2,865), eliminate the chemical facilities inspection program (223 positions) and the 14-position election security program, close the Stakeholder Engagement Division apart from one team, and cut 63 bombing-prevention and school-safety positions; the request is not enacted.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin tells the House Homeland Security Committee CISA will undergo significant structural changes, that a Senate-confirmed director will be nominated (Nick Andersen is acting director), and that the FY2027 budget proposes cutting more than $700 million; the report does not mention relocating CISA or moving its functions to other agencies.

A CRS analysis of the FY2027 DHS request states that CISA's request is 2.49 billion dollars, 109 million above the FY2026 request and 386 million (13.4 percent) below the FY2025 continuing-resolution level, with a research and development account of 44 million dollars partly from moving Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction work to CISA; the text read does not cover election security, counter-misinformation or program eliminations, and says CISA's staffing fell sharply in the six months to March 2026.

OMB Director Russell Vought tells lawmakers he will work with Secretary Mullin on rehiring for CISA, which Mullin has said he wants to expand by 600 staff; acting director Andersen says CISA expects nearly 200 job offers by the end of June.

DHS publishes a Federal Register notice (91 FR 40022) establishing ANCHOR-CI, an advisory body of sector and cross-sector councils that advises the Secretary through the CISA Director; the notice does not mention the Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.

CISA releases its 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan (regional directors as election security advisers, threat-sharing platform); Nextgov notes it does not restore dedicated election adviser positions and that the FY2027 request would eliminate the election security program.

title: Narrow CISA to two core missions and end its counter-disinformation work
uncertainties: Not verified: whether the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee specifically was terminated (reports of the 2025-01-20 DHS memo name only the Cyber Safety Review Board; a Federal Register search for the committee returned no termination or meeting notice); and the date and form of the end of CISA's mis/disinformation work (evidence is staff leave reported in a state official's letter). The FY2027 justification, read from a copy retrieved from dhs.gov on 2026-10-26, contains none of the words misinformation, disinformation or malinformation in the text of its 279 pages, so SecurityWeek's report that the request terminates programs combating misinformation is not supported by the document and is uncorroborated by the two other trade reports of that date. The justification carries no printed date; the source date 2026-04-03 comes from the dhs.gov file path (PDF metadata show creation on 2026-03-31), while trade reports date the request 2026-04-07. Its comparison base is the FY2026 annualized continuing resolution ($2,873,008K), whereas CRS R48979 describes the 386 million dollar gap as below the FY2025 continuing-resolution level (Inference: an annualized continuing resolution at FY2025 rates would make the two consistent; not verified). The basis of SecurityWeek's 707 million dollar figure was not established, and Nextgov's net figure of about 360 million dollars after transfers differs from the document's 385.8 million dollar decrease. The request also moves Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction (280.8 million dollars) into CISA's Infrastructure Security account, so that account rises even as Infrastructure Assessments and Security falls from 112.8 to 65.7 million dollars. The closure of the Stakeholder Engagement Division is reported by Cybersecurity Dive and is not among the points verified from the justification. Page references to the justification come from the reading of the copy. The DHS Budget in Brief (dhs.gov) was not opened. The 2026 staffing figures differ across outlets (about 1,000 positions lost; a target of 2,800 staff reported against about 2,200 currently, which the source itself left unclear). An AOL copy of a report on 12 CISA employees placed on leave returned an error and was not used. Searches run: CSAC termination, CISA election and disinformation staff, CISA director and FY2027 budget; no search found any proposal to move CISA to Transportation.
